## The U-shaped curve has two causes

On [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd), the error on new sites
fell as the tree grew, reached a lowest point, then rose. The fall and the rise have
different causes. This page separates them, and finds a third part of the error that no
model can touch.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## The error on new data splits into bias, variance and noise

Picture the survey repeated many times: the same shelf, the same design, different sites
each time. The same method fitted to each survey gives a slightly different model, and
each model predicts something slightly different at a new station. Set those predictions beside the station's expected count, the average
count the station would give if it could be sampled again and again, and three parts of the
error appear.

- **Bias** is how far the average prediction, over all the surveys, sits from the expected
  count. A model too rigid to follow the pattern misses in the same direction on every
  survey, and more surveys do not help.
- **Variance** is how much the predictions differ from survey to survey. A flexible model
  follows whichever stations it happened to get, so each survey gives it a different shape.
- [Noise](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd#averaging-the-misses-gives-the-objective)
  is how far a single count falls from its expected count. A station expected to
  hold four animals may yield none, or a dozen. No model can predict that part, because it
  does not depend on the inputs.

The squared error at a new station, averaged over many surveys, is the sum of the three
parts:

$$\text{squared error} = \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} + \text{noise}$$

::: {.diagram}
![A rigid model fitted to six surveys gives six similar predictions that all miss the expected count: high bias, low variance. A flexible model gives six predictions that centre on it but disagree: low bias, high variance. Counts at the same spot scatter around the expected count whatever the model. More flexibility trades bias for variance; the noise stays.](img/bias-variance.svg){fig-alt="Three small panels, each with a dashed hump-shaped curve for the expected count and a dotted mark at one station. Rigid model, high bias and low variance: six straight lines fitted to six surveys lie close together, and all miss the top of the hump; a bracket marked bias spans the gap between the curve and the lines. Flexible model, low bias and high variance: six wavy curves follow the hump but spread apart; a bracket marked variance spans their spread. Noise, the same for every model: dots for counts at one station scatter above and below the curve; a bracket marked noise spans them. Below, a wide panel says the error at a new station is bias squared plus variance plus noise, and shows two stacked bars. The rigid model's bar is mostly bias with a little variance; the flexible model's bar is mostly variance with a little bias. Both end in a noise segment of the same length. More flexibility trades bias for variance, and the noise stays the same. A note says bias and variance belong to the model, and the noise belongs to the counts."}
:::

More flexibility lowers the bias and raises the variance. That exchange is the
**bias–variance trade-off**, and it explains the U-shaped error curve: on the way down, bias is
falling faster than variance rises; on the way up, the reverse. The noise is the same
for every model, so it sets a floor that no setting can reach below.

## Worked example

Splitting the error needs two things no real study has: many surveys of the same shelf,
and the expected count at each station. The survey is simulated, so the expected counts
are known; [The coastal survey](../02-marine-data/the-coastal-survey.qmd) introduced them
as the truth file. The many surveys are imitated by drawing many sets of sites from one
pool.

### Preparing the data

A quarter of the training sites are set aside, and every model is judged at their
stations. From the remaining sites, 100 replicate surveys are drawn, each with half of
the sites. The trees are those of [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd),
sized by their minimum node size, `min_n`.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |>
  left_join(load_coastal_survey_truth(), by = "station_id")

split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75)
train <- training(split)

# A quarter of the training sites, where every model is judged
held_out   <- group_initial_split(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75)
pool       <- training(held_out)
evaluation <- testing(held_out)

# 100 replicate surveys, each with half of the remaining sites
surveys <- group_mc_cv(pool, group = site_id, prop = 0.5, times = 100)

predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
  salinity_psu + substrate + season

tree_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors())

tree_model <- function(min_n) {
  decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = 30, min_n = min_n,
                cost_complexity = 0)
}
leaves_of <- function(fitted) sum(extract_fit_engine(fitted)$frame$var == "<leaf>")

c(pool = nrow(pool), evaluation = nrow(evaluation))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean, load_coastal_survey_truth

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean().merge(load_coastal_survey_truth(),
                                           on="station_id")

numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]
categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
predictors = numeric + categorical

grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123)
train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"]))
train = survey.iloc[train_rows]

# A quarter of the training sites, where every model is judged
pool_rows, evaluation_rows = next(grouper.split(train, groups=train["site_id"]))
pool, evaluation = train.iloc[pool_rows], train.iloc[evaluation_rows]

# 100 replicate surveys, each with half of the remaining sites
splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=100, train_size=0.5, random_state=123)
surveys = [rows for rows, _ in splitter.split(pool, groups=pool["site_id"])]

tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric),
    ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False,
                                  handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical),
])

def tree_model(min_n):
    return DecisionTreeRegressor(min_samples_split=min_n,
                                 min_samples_leaf=max(1, round(min_n / 3)),
                                 random_state=123)

pd.Series({"pool": len(pool), "evaluation": len(evaluation)})
```

:::

### Replicate surveys show how much a tree's predictions move

For every replicate survey, trees with 11 minimum node sizes, from 200 down to 2, are
fitted, and each predicts every evaluation station.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: replicates
sizes <- c(200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2)

predict_survey <- function(s, i) {
  one_survey <- analysis(s)
  map(sizes, \(n) {
    fitted <- workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(n)) |> fit(one_survey)
    tibble(survey     = i,
           min_n      = n,
           leaves     = leaves_of(fitted),
           station_id = evaluation$station_id,
           .pred      = predict(fitted, evaluation)$.pred)
  }) |>
    list_rbind()
}

predictions <- imap(surveys$splits, predict_survey) |> list_rbind()
nrow(predictions)
```

## Python

```{python}
sizes = [200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2]

rows = []
for i, survey_rows in enumerate(surveys):
    one_survey = pool.iloc[survey_rows]
    for n in sizes:
        fitted = (Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", tree_model(n))])
                  .fit(one_survey[predictors], one_survey["abundance"]))
        rows.append(pd.DataFrame({
            "survey": i,
            "min_n": n,
            "leaves": fitted["model"].get_n_leaves(),
            "station_id": evaluation["station_id"].to_numpy(),
            "pred": fitted.predict(evaluation[predictors]),
        }))

predictions = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
len(predictions)
```

:::

### Bias and variance come from the spread of predictions at each station

At each evaluation station, the 100 predictions give the two parts that belong to the
model. Their average, set against the expected count, gives the bias; their spread gives
the variance. The noise comes from the counts alone: how far each observed count lies from
its expected count. All three are averaged over the stations.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: decompose
# bias² and variance at each station, then averaged over the stations
split_error <- function(predictions) {
  predictions |>
    left_join(select(evaluation, station_id, true_mean), by = "station_id") |>
    group_by(station_id, .add = TRUE) |>
    summarise(bias_squared = (mean(.pred) - first(true_mean))^2,
              variance     = mean((.pred - mean(.pred))^2),
              .groups = "drop_last") |>
    summarise(across(c(bias_squared, variance), mean))
}

noise <- mean((evaluation$abundance - evaluation$true_mean)^2)

leaves <- predictions |>
  distinct(survey, min_n, leaves) |>
  group_by(min_n) |>
  summarise(leaves = mean(leaves))

parts <- predictions |>
  group_by(min_n) |>
  split_error() |>
  left_join(leaves, by = "min_n") |>
  mutate(noise = noise, total = bias_squared + variance + noise) |>
  relocate(leaves, .after = min_n) |>
  arrange(desc(min_n))

parts |> mutate(across(-min_n, \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
truth = evaluation.set_index("station_id")["true_mean"]

# bias² and variance at each station, then averaged over the stations
def split_error(predictions, by):
    at_station = (predictions.groupby(by + ["station_id"])["pred"]
                  .agg(average="mean", variance=lambda p: p.var(ddof=0))
                  .reset_index())
    at_station["bias_squared"] = (at_station["average"]
                                  - at_station["station_id"].map(truth)) ** 2
    return (at_station.groupby(by, as_index=False)
            [["bias_squared", "variance"]].mean())

noise = ((evaluation["abundance"] - evaluation["true_mean"]) ** 2).mean()

leaves = predictions.groupby("min_n", as_index=False)["leaves"].mean()

parts = (split_error(predictions, ["min_n"])
         .merge(leaves, on="min_n")
         .assign(noise=noise,
                 total=lambda d: d["bias_squared"] + d["variance"] + noise)
         [["min_n", "leaves", "bias_squared", "variance", "noise", "total"]]
         .sort_values("min_n", ascending=False)
         .reset_index(drop=True))

parts.round(2)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: parts-numbers
#| include: false
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
in_words <- function(n) {
  if (n > 10) return(as.character(n))
  c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")[n]
}
parts <- mutate(parts, model_error = bias_squared + variance)
row_at <- function(n) filter(parts, min_n == n)
stiff <- row_at(max(sizes))
loose <- row_at(min(sizes))
lowest_bias <- slice_min(parts, bias_squared)
best <- slice_min(parts, model_error)
noise_share <- round(100 * noise / best$total)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-parts
#| fig-cap: "Bias², variance and their sum against the number of leaves in the tree, from trees fitted to 100 replicate surveys and judged at the same evaluation stations. The dashed line is the noise, which every model carries on top of the other two."
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("Three lines of squared error against the number of leaves on a logarithmic axis. The bias squared line starts at {f2(stiff$bias_squared)} for the most rigid trees, falls to about {f2(lowest_bias$bias_squared)}, then levels off. The variance line starts at {f2(stiff$variance)} and climbs ever faster to {f2(loose$variance)} for the most flexible trees. Their sum is U-shaped, lowest at {f2(best$model_error)} with about {round(best$leaves)} leaves. A dashed line at {f2(noise)} marks the noise, above the sum everywhere except at the flexible end.")
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
parts |>
  select(leaves, `Bias²` = bias_squared, Variance = variance,
         `Bias² + variance` = model_error) |>
  pivot_longer(-leaves, names_to = "part", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(part = fct_inorder(part)) |>
  ggplot(aes(leaves, value, colour = part)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = noise, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = min(parts$leaves), y = noise + 0.8, hjust = 0, size = 3.4,
           colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], label = "noise: the same for every model") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(ml_palette[c("blue", "vermilion", "green")])) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(x = "Leaves in the tree (log scale)", y = "Squared error (individuals²)",
       colour = NULL, title = "Bias falls and stops; variance keeps rising")
```

:::

### Bias falling and variance rising make the U

**Bias falls, then stops.** The most rigid trees, with about
`r in_words(round(stiff$leaves))` leaves, give very different stations the same
prediction, and have a bias² of `r f2(stiff$bias_squared)`. Bigger trees bring it down to
about `r f2(lowest_bias$bias_squared)` by about `r round(lowest_bias$leaves)` leaves, and
no further. What remains is a shape that trees on these inputs cannot reach, however
finely they cut.

**Variance keeps rising.** A leaf predicts the average count of its stations, and more
leaves mean fewer stations in each. An average of a few counts depends on which stations
a survey happened to catch, so the variance grows from `r f2(stiff$variance)` to
`r f2(loose$variance)`, faster at each step.

**Their sum is the U-shaped error curve.** Bias² plus variance is lowest, at `r f2(best$model_error)`, for a
node size of `r best$min_n`, about `r in_words(round(best$leaves))` leaves. To the left, bias costs
more than variance saves; to the right, the reverse.

**For the best tree, the noise is the largest part.** The noise is `r f2(noise)`, about
`r in_words(round(noise / best$model_error))` times the bias² and variance of the best
tree, and `r noise_share`% of its whole error. A model with no bias and no
variance at all would still have an RMSE of `r f2(sqrt(noise))`. That is why the best tree
on [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd) beat predicting the average by so
little: most of what is left is chance in the counts, which no model removes.

No real study can draw this chart, because no real survey knows its expected counts. In
practice only the sum shows, as the error on new sites on
[Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd).

### Averaging trees cuts the variance

[Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) built a
forest by averaging many trees. The same decomposition shows what the averaging does. Here
a forest of 100 trees, each with a node size of 5, is fitted to the same 100 replicate surveys and
set beside a single tree with the same node size.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: forest
forest_model <- rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 100, min_n = 5) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 123)

forest_predictions <- imap(surveys$splits, \(s, i) {
  fitted <- workflow(tree_recipe, forest_model) |> fit(analysis(s))
  tibble(survey = i, station_id = evaluation$station_id,
         .pred = predict(fitted, evaluation)$.pred)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

tree_and_forest <- bind_rows(
  `single tree` = filter(predictions, min_n == 5),
  `random forest` = forest_predictions,
  .id = "model"
) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  split_error()

tree_and_forest |> mutate(across(-model, \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
rows = []
for i, survey_rows in enumerate(surveys):
    one_survey = pool.iloc[survey_rows]
    # max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does.
    forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, max_features="sqrt",
                                   min_samples_split=5, random_state=123,
                                   n_jobs=-1)
    fitted = (Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", forest)])
              .fit(one_survey[predictors], one_survey["abundance"]))
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({
        "survey": i,
        "station_id": evaluation["station_id"].to_numpy(),
        "pred": fitted.predict(evaluation[predictors]),
    }))

tree_and_forest = pd.concat([
    predictions.query("min_n == 5").assign(model="single tree"),
    pd.concat(rows).assign(model="random forest"),
])

split_error(tree_and_forest, ["model"]).round(2)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: forest-numbers
#| include: false
one_tree <- filter(tree_and_forest, model == "single tree")
forest <- filter(tree_and_forest, model == "random forest")
```

The forest's bias² is `r f2(forest$bias_squared)`, against `r f2(one_tree$bias_squared)`
for the single tree: its trees are the same kind of tree, so averaging them leaves the
bias where it was. Its variance is `r f2(forest$variance)` against
`r f2(one_tree$variance)`: the single tree's is about
`r in_words(round(one_tree$variance / forest$variance))` times as large. Each tree
still follows its own stations, but the trees follow different ones, and their mistakes
partly cancel in the average.

[Regularisation](regularisation.qmd) goes the other way: it adds a little bias on purpose,
to cut more variance than it costs.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- Over many surveys, the squared error at a new station splits into **bias²**, the average
  model's systematic miss; **variance**, how much the model changes from survey to
  survey; and noise, how far a count falls from its expected count.
- More flexibility lowers the bias and raises the variance, and their sum is the U-shaped
  error curve. On the survey, the noise was larger than the bias² and variance of the best
  tree put together: most of the error was chance that no model removes.
- A random forest keeps the bias of its trees and cuts their variance by averaging them.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Give each replicate survey three quarters of the pool's sites instead of half, by
   setting `prop = 0.75` in `group_mc_cv()`. Before running it, decide which part should
   change most, bias² or variance, and whether the best tree should get bigger or smaller.
2. Add a linear regression to the comparison of the tree and the forest: in the forest
   code, replace `forest_model` with `linear_reg()`. Is a straight-line model's error
   mostly bias or mostly variance?
